prompt: Lesson 6 wrote SQL and Go by hand, lesson 7 let GORM write the SQL. What does sqlc change?
hint: Who writes which half?

choices.text: You write the SQL; a program writes the Go
choices.why: Right. The queries stay yours, and the scanning code is generated from them.

choices.text: You write structs; sqlc writes the SQL from them at run time
choices.why: That describes an ORM such as GORM, the opposite direction.

choices.text: Both halves are still written by hand, with a linter between them
choices.why: The Go half is generated; nobody keeps it in step by hand.

choices.text: sqlc replaces pgx as the driver
choices.why: The generated code calls pgx; sqlc is not a driver.

prompt: When does sqlc itself run?
hint: Is it imported by boxoffice?

choices.text: On every request, to build the query
choices.why: Nothing of sqlc runs inside the server; only the code it left behind.

choices.text: When the server starts, to read queries.sql from disk
choices.why: The SQL is copied into the generated Go file; the server reads no .sql file.

choices.text: Inside PostgreSQL, as a stored procedure that the driver calls on each query
choices.why: sqlc is a program on your machine, not something installed in the database.

choices.text: Before go build, like a compiler
choices.why: Right. It writes ordinary Go that is checked in beside the code that calls it.

prompt: Match each input of the pipeline to what it says.
hint: Three files go in.

pairs.right: each query, with a name and what it returns
where the other two are and what to generate

right_distractors: the HTTP routes of the service

prompt: Why does `go install` of sqlc need a C compiler when most Go tools do not?
hint: How does sqlc understand PostgreSQL's SQL?

choices.text: It generates C files instead of Go
choices.why: The output is Go; the C is inside sqlc itself.

choices.text: Go 1.27 compiles every module through gcc
choices.why: Pure Go builds without gcc; only cgo needs it.

choices.text: It embeds PostgreSQL's C parser via cgo
choices.why: Right. cgo is Go's bridge to C, and it needs a C compiler to build.

choices.text: The gcc package carries PostgreSQL's headers
choices.why: gcc is the compiler; the parser's source comes with sqlc's module.

prompt: Why install `sqlc@v1.31.1` rather than `sqlc@latest`?
hint: Look at the top of a generated file.

choices.text: `@latest` is refused by go install
choices.why: It is accepted; it is just not reproducible.

choices.text: Later releases need a newer gcc
choices.why: The lesson says nothing about that; the argument is reproducible output.

choices.text: Generated files record the version that made them
choices.why: Right. Pinning keeps every machine producing the same files.

choices.text: v1.31.1 is the only release that supports pgx/v5
choices.why: The lesson pins it for consistency, not because others lack pgx support.

prompt: The build stops with `cgo: C compiler "gcc" not found` in `runtime/cgo`. What is the fix on Ubuntu?
hint: Read the message to its end.

choices.text: Set `CGO_ENABLED=1`
choices.why: cgo was already trying; it found no compiler to run.

choices.text: `sudo apt install -y gcc`
choices.why: Right. One package, and lesson 15's race detector needs it too.

choices.text: Reinstall Go from the archive
choices.why: Go is fine; the C compiler is what is missing.

choices.text: Run go install as root with sudo
choices.why: Permissions are not the problem; the compiler does not exist.

prompt: In `queries.sql`, what does the line `-- name: SellSeats :one` do?
hint: It is not an ordinary comment.

choices.text: Nothing; SQL ignores comments
choices.why: PostgreSQL ignores it, sqlc reads it.

choices.text: Marks the query to run once at start-up
choices.why: :one is about rows returned, not how often it runs.

choices.text: Names the Go function and says it returns one row
choices.why: Right. The annotation decides the function's name and its result.

choices.text: Restricts the query to a single connection of the pool
choices.why: The pool is not mentioned by the annotation.

prompt: Match each annotation to what the generated function returns.
hint: Four annotations from the table.

pairs.right: a slice, empty when there are no rows
the rows affected, and an error

prompt: In `SellSeats`, why is the quantity written `sqlc.arg(quantity)` instead of `$1`?
hint: What does sqlc name a `$1` after?

choices.text: It is compared with an expression, not a column, so sqlc has no column to name it after; the same name twice is one parameter
choices.why: Right. It becomes the field Quantity of SellSeatsParams.

choices.text: PostgreSQL rejects `$1` in an UPDATE
choices.why: The generated SQL uses `$1`; PostgreSQL accepts it.

choices.text: `sqlc.arg` makes the parameter optional
choices.why: That is `sqlc.narg`, section 08.

choices.text: To keep the value out of the SQL text
choices.why: `$1` keeps it out as well; this is about naming.

prompt: Code under a directory called ___ can only be imported from inside the same module, which is why sqlc's output goes there.
hint: The `out` of sqlc.yaml begins with it.

prompt: How many lines of Go did `sqlc generate` write, across its three files?
hint: The `wc -l` total.

prompt: Why are the fields of the generated `Event` `int32` while boxoffice's own `Event` uses `int`?
hint: Where does sqlc take the types from?

choices.text: sqlc rounds every number down to save memory
choices.why: It follows the column type, nothing else.

choices.text: pgx/v5 has no 64-bit integer
choices.why: pgx handles bigint fine; the column here is 32-bit.

choices.text: sqlc.yaml asks for int32
choices.why: The configuration says nothing about integer sizes.

choices.text: The columns are 32-bit `integer`
choices.why: Right. Types come from the table, and section 06 converts between the two.

prompt: What lets the same generated `Queries` run through a pool, a single connection or a transaction?
hint: Look at db.go.

choices.text: A type switch inside every generated function that tests for each of the three
choices.why: The generated functions only call q.db; no switch exists.

choices.text: A global variable set by main
choices.why: Queries holds its DBTX as a field; nothing is global.

choices.text: Reflection on the value passed to New
choices.why: It is an ordinary interface; no reflection is involved.

choices.text: The `DBTX` interface, three methods all of them have
choices.why: Right. New wraps any of them, and WithTx swaps in a transaction.

prompt: A generated file starts with `Code generated by sqlc. DO NOT EDIT.` You need its SQL changed. What do you do?
hint: Where does the file come from?

choices.text: Edit it, and commit before anyone regenerates
choices.why: The next `sqlc generate` silently undoes the edit.

choices.text: Copy it to a new file and edit the copy
choices.why: Then the copy drifts from the SQL, the problem sqlc removes.

choices.text: Change queries.sql, then regenerate
choices.why: Right. A generated file is changed through its inputs.

choices.text: Delete the header line, then edit freely
choices.why: The header is a warning, not a lock; removing it does not stop regeneration.

prompt: With the first sqlc version of `pgStore`, `GET /events/4294967297` answered with the Jazz at the Docks. Why?

choices.text: PostgreSQL rounds ids that are too large
choices.why: PostgreSQL was asked for event 1, correctly; the change happened in Go.

choices.text: `int32(id)` kept the low 32 bits, which are 1
choices.why: Right. Go defines the conversion as a wrap-around: no panic, no log.

choices.text: strconv.Atoi reads only the last digit
choices.why: Atoi returned 4294967297 exactly; the conversion afterwards wrapped it.

choices.text: The mux matched the longest prefix, /events/1
choices.why: The wildcard took the whole segment; the mux has no such rule.

prompt: Lesson 6's hand-written store got the same request and did not answer with event 1. What happened there?
hint: Which type did it pass to pgx?

choices.text: A 404, because pgx returned ErrNoRows
choices.why: pgx refused to encode the value, so no query ran and no row was looked for.

choices.text: The store converted to int32 too, and returned event 1
choices.why: It passed the int unconverted; that is the difference.

choices.text: pgx refused the value; a 500
choices.why: Right. Not the right answer, but not somebody else's event either.

choices.text: The validation of lesson 3 refused ids above 10
choices.why: Validation covers quantity and e-mail, not the path id.

prompt: What does the fixed store do with an id above `math.MaxInt32`?
hint: Read `eventID`.

choices.text: Clamps it to MaxInt32 and queries that
choices.why: That would answer for another event again.

choices.text: Panics, and the recoverPanics middleware turns it into a 500 response
choices.why: It returns an error; nothing panics.

choices.text: Returns ErrNotFound at once
choices.why: Right. No such event can exist in an int4 column, so 404 is the truth.

choices.text: Converts it to int64 for the query
choices.why: The generated function takes int32; the store refuses instead.

prompt: When `pgStore` switched to sqlc, which files of boxoffice changed besides `pgstore.go`?
hint: What did the handlers ever see?

choices.text: Every handler, to call the generated functions
choices.why: Handlers call the Store; the store calls the generated code.

choices.text: main.go, to build a db.Queries for the routes
choices.why: pgStore builds it itself in q(); main keeps &pgStore{pool: pool}.

choices.text: routes.go, which now takes a *db.Queries in place of the Store
choices.why: routes still takes a Store.

choices.text: None of the handlers, routes or main
choices.why: Right. They only saw the Store interface.

prompt: With the configuration of section 04, `sould` typed for `sold` inside the WHERE of `SellSeats`. When was it found?
hint: Follow the transcript.

choices.text: At sqlc generate
choices.why: generate and go build both succeeded; that is the point.

choices.text: At the first purchase
choices.why: Right. PostgreSQL refused it with SQLSTATE 42703.

choices.text: At go build
choices.why: The column name is inside a string of SQL; the compiler does not read it.

choices.text: At go vet, as a warning
choices.why: vet does not read SQL either.

prompt: PostgreSQL refused the misspelled column with SQLSTATE ___, undefined column.
hint: Five characters, in the log line.

prompt: What did adding `database: uri: ${DATABASE_URL}` to sqlc.yaml change?
hint: Who checks the queries now?

choices.text: sqlc prepares every query against PostgreSQL during generate, so the typo became a generate error
choices.why: Right. queries.sql:15:12, before any Go was built.

choices.text: The server connects with that URL instead of its own
choices.why: The server still reads DATABASE_URL in main; the block is for sqlc.

choices.text: sqlc applies schema.sql to the database
choices.why: It asks the database; the tables must already exist.

choices.text: Generated code stores the address
choices.why: The address is read from the environment, never written.

prompt: `env -u DATABASE_URL sqlc generate` failed to connect. What does that tell you about the database-backed check?
hint: Think of a continuous integration machine.

choices.text: It is optional at generate time and skipped when no database answers
choices.why: generate did not skip; it failed.

choices.text: sqlc caches the last schema and uses it next time
choices.why: Nothing cached it; the run failed.

choices.text: It only works for the user postgres
choices.why: It connected as ana and asked for database ana; the URL was missing.

choices.text: The database must exist, with the tables, wherever generate runs
choices.why: Right. In CI that means a PostgreSQL beside the build.

prompt: `WHERE seats - sold >= $1` is mistyped as `<=` in SellSeats. Which check catches it?
hint: Is it valid SQL?

choices.text: sqlc's static analysis
choices.why: The SQL is valid; there is nothing to flag.

choices.text: The database-backed analysis
choices.why: PostgreSQL prepares it without complaint.

choices.text: go vet's printf check
choices.why: vet reads Go, not SQL meaning.

choices.text: A test
choices.why: Right. sqlc checks the SQL means something; only tests check it means the right thing.

prompt: Why is a search with optional filters awkward for sqlc?
hint: When must the SQL exist?

choices.text: Each function is one fixed statement
choices.why: Right. It cannot add a condition per filter at run time, as an ORM does.

choices.text: sqlc rejects ILIKE
choices.why: SearchEvents uses ILIKE and generates cleanly.

choices.text: pgx cannot send NULL
choices.why: pgtype.Int4 with Valid false is sent as NULL.

choices.text: Query parameters cannot reach a :many query
choices.why: Any value reaches it as a parameter; the SQL shape is the issue.

prompt: In `(sqlc.narg(min_available)::int IS NULL OR seats - sold >= sqlc.narg(min_available)::int)`, what happens when the filter is not given?
hint: Evaluate the left half.

choices.text: The query fails, because NULL cannot be compared
choices.why: The left half is true, so the comparison does not matter.

choices.text: Every row passes it
choices.why: Right. A missing filter filters nothing.

choices.text: No row passes, because NULL is false
choices.why: `IS NULL` of a NULL is true, not NULL.

choices.text: sqlc removes the condition from the generated SQL
choices.why: The SQL is fixed; the database evaluates it.

prompt: Over millions of rows, why can the single optional-filter query be slow where separate queries are fast?
hint: How many times is it planned?

choices.text: NULL parameters cost a round trip each
choices.why: Parameters travel together with the query.

choices.text: ILIKE disables every index in PostgreSQL
choices.why: The lesson's argument is about the shared plan, not ILIKE.

choices.text: One plan must cover every combination, so an index that suits one filter goes unused
choices.why: Right. Write the common combinations separately, or build that one statement at run time.

choices.text: pgtype.Text is slower to decode than string
choices.why: Decoding is not the cost the lesson names.

prompt: Match each approach to where its SQL can be read.
hint: The third row of the table.

pairs.right: in queries.sql and in the generated file

prompt: Which are true of sqlc and not of pgx by hand? Choose all that apply.
hint: Rows of the comparison table.

choices.text: A column and a field cannot get out of step
choices.why: Right. Both are generated together.

choices.text: A misspelled column is found at generate, with a database to ask
choices.why: Right. By hand it is found when the query runs.

choices.text: Its new modules include GORM
choices.why: sqlc's generated code needs pgx only.

choices.text: It needs an extra tool and gcc to build that tool
choices.why: Right. pgx by hand needs no extra tool.

choices.text: Optional filters are natural
choices.why: That is GORM's column; for sqlc they are awkward.

prompt: A team is building an admin screen with fifty optional search filters over one big table. What does the lesson's comparison point to?
hint: Where is sqlc awkward?

choices.text: Weigh a query builder or an ORM
choices.why: Right. The lesson says such a service would weigh the trade differently.

choices.text: sqlc, because generated code is fastest
choices.why: Speed was never the argument; optional filters are sqlc's weak spot.

choices.text: pgx by hand with values pasted into the SQL string
choices.why: Values never go into the SQL text; lesson 6 section 07.

choices.text: No database at all
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson suggests dropping the database.

prompt: Put the steps of changing a query in boxoffice in order, from editing to a running server.
hint: The generated code comes from queries.sql.
items: Run sqlc generate, which asks PostgreSQL about it
Adjust pgstore.go to the new generated signature
go build, then start the server
trap: Never start by editing internal/db by hand.

prompt: A new column `price` is added to the table as `bigint`, and to the queries. Where should you look first for a bug like section 06's?
hint: Compare the generated type with boxoffice's own.

choices.text: In the generated file, which must be edited
choices.why: Generated files are not edited; the conversion is yours.

choices.text: At the conversion lines
choices.why: Right. A bigint maps to int64; storing it in a narrower Go type wraps silently.

choices.text: In the mux patterns
choices.why: The mux knows nothing about column types.

choices.text: In sqlc.yaml's database block
choices.why: That block checks names and types against PostgreSQL, not Go conversions.
